draft.title: Megacities and urban corridors
card: a city with more than 10 million people. The count usually includes the built-up areas around the city, not only the centre.
a chain of cities and towns that have grown towards each other. Together they form one long built-up strip.
Los Angeles and its surrounds is a megacity. The strip of cities from Boston to Washington on the east coast of the United States is an urban corridor.
A megacity is defined by its size. An urban corridor is defined by its shape and the links between its cities. Some places can be both.
draft.remember: Megacity: over 10 million people. Urban corridor: cities joined in a chain.

a.q: Which description fits an urban corridor?
opts: A chain of cities that have grown together
A single city with more than 10 million people
A city that is growing faster than the countryside
A city with a large area of farmland around it
a.why: An urban corridor is a chain of cities joined into one strip. The option about 10 million people describes a megacity, which is about size, not shape.
a.clue: Think of cities linked like beads on a string.

b.q: Region X has five cities of about 3 million people each. They sit along a coast and their suburbs now touch. Which term best fits Region X?
opts: An urban corridor
A megacity
A rural region
A single suburb
b.why: The cities form a joined chain, so it is an urban corridor. It is not a megacity, because no single city has more than 10 million people. Adding up the total does not make it one city.
b.clue: Check whether any one city passes 10 million.

a.best: A chain of cities that have grown together

problems.detail: The card says a megacity's count usually includes the built-up areas around the city, and that some places can be both. Five cities of about 3 million whose suburbs touch form one continuous built-up area of about 15 million. Under that agglomeration reading, 'A megacity' is defensible, so the question does not have a single clear right answer.

The why says 'Adding up the total does not make it one city.' The card does not teach this rule, and it sits uneasily with the card's own points that megacity counts include surrounding built-up areas and that some places can be both.

check.summary: Question a is sound. In question b the joined cities total about 15 million, so 'megacity' is defensible under the card's own counting rule and its 'some places can be both' line. The why also relies on a rule the card never teaches.
